title: Ukraine’s Attacks on Russian Data Centers Lay Bare a Global Risk to AI | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Martin argues Ukraine's drone strikes on Yandex and Sberbank data centers, and Iran's earlier strikes on AWS facilities in the UAE and Bahrain, expose the physical vulnerability of AI infrastructure, and recommends redundancy, data portability and edge computing.

themes.theme: Ukraine's strikes on Russian data centers

insights.claim: Ukrainian drones destroyed three Yandex data centers, severely disrupting emails, payments and navigation across Russia, and later hit a Sberbank data center under construction.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: Cloud concentration creates national-scale outage risk.
insights.locator: Last week, Ukrainian drones took out three data centers

insights.claim: The strikes will have minimal effect on the global AI race since Russia lags three to five years behind the US and China, but they set back Russian AI because Yandex's supercomputers run on Nvidia A100 chips that are hard to replace.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: Chip export controls make physical losses hard for Russia to replace.
insights.locator: Even so, Ukraine’s drone strikes will likely still set back

insights.claim: In March, Iranian drones struck two AWS data centers in the UAE and damaged one in Bahrain, causing physical, power and fire-suppression water damage, and in September AWS said it could not restore data hosted exclusively at two of them.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: Gulf cloud regions carry real physical risk; customers need multi-region backups.
insights.locator: This was already apparent in March of this year

insights.claim: Iran's security chief warned that if fighting resumes, data centers and connected subsea cables would be targets, and Middle East siting risk is reflected in rising insurance costs; Stargate UAE is reportedly under review.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: Expect higher insurance and a risk discount on Gulf AI data center projects.
insights.locator: Even though AWS has committed to replacing damaged equipment

insights.claim: Data centers are an especially vulnerable node in AI's attack surface because they are large, fixed in location, and integrated systems where an attack on power or cooling can render the whole facility inoperable.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: Physical concentration of AI compute is a systemic risk to AI-linked valuations.
insights.locator: Whether they are located in Russia, Ukraine, the Gulf or elsewhere

insights.claim: Industry physical security standards address unauthorized intrusion, not missiles and drones, so options for hardening against air attack are limited.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: Hardening spend against kinetic threats is a gap and potential market.
insights.locator: The options for hardening data center defenses are limited

insights.claim: Companies and nations should pursue redundancy and resiliency, starting with data portability; Russia's strict localization law left few options, while Ukrainian providers survived by backing up to EU servers.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
entities: EU Cloud and AI Development Act
insights.so_what: Data localization rules carry resilience costs; multi-region architectures gain value.
insights.locator: Russia’s strict data localization law leaves it few options

insights.claim: Edge computing can disperse processing across smaller sites, but it cannot replace AI training or supercomputers whose performance depends on scale, while underground or space data centers remain years from viability.
insights.speaker: Connor Martin
insights.so_what: Edge helps serving resilience but not frontier training concentration.
insights.locator: Another way to bolster resiliency is to invest in edge computing
